claims.claim: for white perch in a lake only Oneida's long larval series exists, in a paywalled paper (VanDeValk et al. 2016)
claims.note: full text not obtained. The abstract confirms a 44-year Oneida series of first-year white perch density from Miller high-speed sampler (larvae) and trawl surveys, with recruitment from gill nets; the article is paywalled (403 at OUP and Wiley, below). Whether it reports larval densities per m³ could not be seen

claims.claim: Oneida's dense larval year classes grew more slowly and died faster, but 'mortality did not compensate for the higher initial densities' (VanDeValk et al. 2016, abstract)
claims.note: not read in full. The abstract's words: 'Year-classes with higher first-year densities grew slower and experienced higher mortality, but mortality did not compensate for the higher initial densities'. It says FIRST-YEAR densities, not larval densities; the paper's 'dense larval year classes' should follow the abstract's wording

claims.claim: recruitment was best explained by larval density together with predator biomass (VanDeValk et al. 2016, abstract)
claims.note: not read in full. The abstract: 'The model that best explained White Perch recruitment to the adult stock was composed of larval density and predator biomass' (AICc model comparison)

notes: Needs the article (doi:10.1080/00028487.2015.1131743, via a library login); it is the source the research notes want for Oneida white perch larval and juvenile densities and first-year Z vs density. The abstract also says year classes dense as larvae tended to be dense as juveniles and to recruit more, and that year-class strength is 'at least partly determined at the larval stage or earlier'. Until read, keep '(abstract)' on every use.
